secret-party.title: The secret party
secret-party.conceptExplain: When someone says “don’t tell anyone,” they’re often protecting the plan — not you. Real friends and safe plans can survive a parent knowing.
secret-party.situation: Mary gets a DM at 11pm: “Warehouse party tonight. Free gifts at the door. No parents. Keep it between us 🤫.” The account followed her yesterday and has cool party photos.
secret-party.question: Who should Mary talk to first?
secret-party.lesson: Secrecy + strangers + “free stuff” is a classic lure. A trusted adult is the first call — not another unknown account.

mom.name: Her mom
clues: Can look at the chat with her
Might ask questions Mary finds awkward
mom.feedback: Best. Awkward questions beat a trap. Show her the DM — “no parents” + free gifts + a brand-new account is exactly what adults are for.

party-acc.name: Party.VIP
clues: Answers fast and hypes her up
party-acc.feedback: Unsafe. This is the account selling the invite. Asking them “is it safe?” is like asking a scammer if the scam is real.

online-friend.name: Lex
online-friend.feedback: Unsafe. Feeling close online ≠ knowing someone in real life. Lex pushing her to go is not a safety plan.

fake-scout.title: The model scout
fake-scout.conceptExplain: Real jobs and agencies don’t rush teens in DMs for their address. Flattery + urgency + “exclusive” is how fake “scouts” get personal info.
fake-scout.situation: A DM: “Hey, you have a look. I’m a scout — fill this form tonight with your address for exclusive castings. Don’t overthink it.” Mary feels flattered… and unsure.
fake-scout.question: Who is safest to trust with checking this?
fake-scout.lesson: Cold DMs that want your address “tonight” aren’t opportunities. Verify with someone who has a duty to protect you — not with the sender.

teacher.name: Ms. de Vries
teacher.feedback: Best. Teachers (and parents) can check if an agency is real. The “scout” should never be the person who proves the scout is legit.

cousin.name: Cousin Ana
clues: Wants to help Mary feel special
cousin.feedback: Partly. Ana cares — but excitement isn’t verification. Still loop in a parent or teacher so someone checks it properly.

scout.name: Elena
clues: Sends a form link for her address
scout.feedback: Unsafe. Never trust the person making the offer to prove it’s safe. Address + urgency in a cold DM is a hard no.

live-pin.title: The ride offer
live-pin.conceptExplain: Asking for your live location, offering a private car, and saying “don’t tell your parents” is about getting you alone — not about being helpful.
live-pin.situation: Mary is finishing homework at the library. A DM: “It’s dark — I’ll pick you up. Drop your live location, I’ll be there in 10. Don’t bother your parents, I’ve got you.”
live-pin.question: Who should Mary trust for getting home?
live-pin.lesson: Live pin + stranger + car = getting you alone. Help comes from people you already know offline.

dad.name: Her dad
dad.feedback: Best. A slow safe ride beats a fast unknown one. Call or text dad — never send a live pin to someone she doesn’t know.

library-staff.name: Library desk staff
clues: Can wait with her or call home
library-staff.feedback: Partly right. Staff can help her reach a parent and keep her in a public place. Still don’t reply to the stranger.

stranger.name: Mike
clues: Sounds worried about her walking alone
stranger.feedback: Unsafe. “Helpful” + live pin + “don’t tell parents” is a classic isolation move — not kindness.

private-pic.title: Prove you trust me
private-pic.conceptExplain: People who care about you don’t need a private photo to “prove trust.” Moving to Snap + “delete it after” + “don’t tell” is pressure, not romance.
private-pic.situation: A follower Mary barely knows: “Add me on Snap. Send a quick pic so I know you’re real. I’ll delete it. Don’t make it weird — and don’t tell anyone.”
private-pic.question: Who should Mary trust with this?
private-pic.lesson: Private apps + photo tests are how some people push for more control. Trust people who protect your privacy — not people who demand it.

parent.name: A parent / carer
clues: Won’t ask Mary for the photo
parent.feedback: Best. Embarrassment is temporary. Show them the chat: no photo, no app switch — adult help first.

bestie.name: Sophia
clues: Is also 14 and might not know how to report
bestie.feedback: Partly. Friends are great for support — for photo pressure, also tell a trusted adult so it gets reported properly.

follower.name: Jaden
follower.feedback: Unsafe. The person asking for a “trust pic” is the risk. “I’ll delete it” is a promise you can’t check.

fake-classmate.title: The fake classmate
fake-classmate.conceptExplain: Accounts can pretend to be someone from your school. Always check through a way you already know (in person, old chat, teacher) — never by giving the new account what it wants.
fake-classmate.situation: “Maya from 4B” DMs: “hey add me to the class WhatsApp — send your number?” Mary sits near Maya in class… but this account looks new, and Mary doesn’t remember chatting like this.
fake-classmate.question: What’s the safest way to check this?
fake-classmate.lesson: Impersonation is common. Verify through people and chats you already trust — never through the suspicious account.

real-maya.name: Maya (known chat / at school)
clues: Mary can ask her tomorrow in class
They already have an old group chat
real-maya.feedback: Best. Ask the real Maya on a channel Mary already uses. If it’s fake, tell a teacher so others don’t get tricked.

ignore.name: Ignore it and say nothing
clues: Nobody else learns the account is fake
ignore.feedback: Partly. Not sharing her number is smart — but telling a teacher/parent helps stop the fake account from targeting the next person.

fake.name: maya.4b.new
clues: Uses Maya’s name and school year
fake.feedback: Unsafe. You don’t “verify” a suspicious account by giving it personal details. That’s the trap.

owe-me.title: You owe me
owe-me.conceptExplain: A free gift that comes with “you owe me” and “don’t tell your parents” isn’t kindness — it’s a hook. You never owe favours for something you didn’t ask to repay.
owe-me.situation: Someone in Mary’s game bought her a battle pass. Then: “lol ur gonna owe me one 😉 just don’t tell your parents ok.” Later they ask her to stay on voice chat late.
owe-me.question: Who should Mary trust about this?
owe-me.lesson: Gifts that create secret debt are a trap. Adults help break the “you owe me” story — the giver doesn’t get to set the rules.

parents.name: Her parents
clues: Can say clearly she owes nothing
Might limit game chat for a bit
Care more about her than the battle pass
parents.feedback: Best. Tell them. A gift never means she has to do favours — especially secret ones. Blocking is allowed.

gamer-friend.name: Theo
gamer-friend.role: Friend from school + the same game
clues: Can’t change her account settings for her
gamer-friend.feedback: Partly. Theo is good backup — still tell a parent, because the secrecy (“don’t tell”) was part of the pressure.

giver.name: SquadMate_x
giver.feedback: Unsafe. Negotiating with the person using gift-debt feeds the trap. She doesn’t owe a chat, a pic, or a secret.

job-abroad.title: The abroad job
job-abroad.conceptExplain: “Quick cash abroad, no ID, leave this week, keep it private” is not a normal teen job. Those lines show up in trafficking and scam ads because they skip every safety check.
job-abroad.situation: Sophia shows Mary a flashy story: “Earn fast abroad — no ID needed, flights this week, privacy guaranteed 💰✈️.” It looks exciting. Both of them feel curious.
job-abroad.question: Who should they trust to handle this?
job-abroad.lesson: Jobs that skip ID and rush travel are danger signals. School adults and official helplines beat the poster’s “privacy.”

teacher.name: Their teacher
clues: Can report it so others see a warning
Might make it a whole-class talk
teacher.feedback: Best. Bring the screenshot to a teacher. Checking with a helpline protects more students than a quiet DM ever will.

sophia-plan.name: Just Sophia — research together
clues: They can Google the company name
Two teens can still miss red flags
sophia-plan.feedback: Partly. Researching together is better than clicking alone — still tell a teacher/parent. Abroad + no ID needs an adult, not just Google.

poster.name: internships.fast
poster.feedback: Unsafe. Never ask the poster of a too-good overseas job to “explain” it. That’s how people get pulled in deeper.

threat.title: The threat
threat.conceptExplain: If someone threatens you after you refuse (photos, money, “everyone will see”), that’s coercion — using fear to control you. You don’t have to handle it alone, and you shouldn’t pay or send more.
threat.situation: Mary said no to a photo. The account replies: “Delete me and you’ll regret it. Everyone at school will see.” She’s scared and staring at the screen.
threat.question: Who should Mary trust for help right now?
threat.lesson: Threats after a no are about fear and control. Don’t pay, don’t argue alone — a trusted adult and a helpline first.

adult-helpline.name: Trusted adult + helpline
clues: Know not to pay or send more
Mary might cry or feel ashamed — that’s okay
adult-helpline.feedback: Best. Stop replying, keep evidence, tell an adult. In the Netherlands: 0800‑0432 (De Kindertelefoon) or helpwanted.nl.

delete-alone.name: Delete everything alone
clues: Leaves her stuck with the fear
delete-alone.feedback: Partly. Stopping the chat helps — but screenshot first and tell an adult. Threats feel smaller when you’re not alone with them.

threatener.name: The account threatening her
threatener.feedback: Unsafe. Paying, arguing, or pleading usually makes it worse. Don’t give them more attention or more content.

jealous-friends.title: Cut your friends off
jealous-friends.conceptExplain: “Your friends are jealous — you only need me” is how control starts. People who care about you don’t ask you to drop your whole support network.
jealous-friends.situation: Someone Mary chats with every day says: “Your friends are jealous of us. Stop hanging out with them. You have me — that’s enough.” Lately they get annoyed when she’s with Sophia.
jealous-friends.question: Who should Mary trust?
jealous-friends.lesson: Isolation often starts soft: “they don’t get us.” Real care never needs you to lose your friends.

friends.name: Her real-life friends
clues: Don’t ask her to hide from her parents
friends.feedback: Best. Keep her friends — and tell them (and a parent) what this person is saying. Isolation shrinks when it’s spoken out loud.

balance.name: Stay quiet and “balance both”
balance.feedback: Partly — keeping friends matters. Still name the behaviour to someone she trusts, so it doesn’t escalate in private.

isolator.name: The chat partner
clues: Gets cold when she’s with friends
isolator.feedback: Unsafe. Anyone who needs her to cut friends off is building control — not a healthier relationship.

safe-study.title: The study invite
safe-study.concept: Not every message is a trap
safe-study.conceptExplain: Safety skills aren’t “trust nobody.” Known classmates, public places, and normal plans can be fine. The skill is spotting pressure, secrecy, and strangers — not freezing your whole life.
safe-study.situation: Maya from biology — Mary sits next to her in class — texts on their usual chat: “Library after school to revise the quiz? I’ll be by the windows. Bring snacks if you want.”
safe-study.question: What’s reasonable here?
safe-study.lesson: Known classmates + a public place + no secrecy can be normal. Still tell a parent where you’re going — that’s ordinary safety, not panic.

maya.name: Maya
maya.feedback: Best. This looks like a normal school plan. Still tell a parent where she’s going — that’s everyday safety, not suspicion.

skip-all.name: Cancel — trust nobody online ever
skip-all.feedback: Partly. Caution is smart — but a known classmate and a public study plan aren’t the same as a groomer DM. Panic isn’t the skill; judgment is.

stranger-offer.name: A random “tutor” DM
clues: Offers free help the same afternoon
Wants to move off the school chat
stranger-offer.feedback: Unsafe. Don’t swap a known classmate plan for a stranger’s “help,” especially if they want a private pickup.
